articles.title: A Searchable Interview Index Without a Complicated System
articles.excerpt: A notebook can hold a wonderful conversation and still hide it from its owner. I remember the subject, the setting, perhaps even the weather, but not which file contains the detail I need. For a busin…
articles.body: A notebook can hold a wonderful conversation and still hide it from its owner. I remember the subject, the setting, perhaps even the weather, but not which file contains the detail I need. For a business feature writer, that is a practical problem. Good material becomes harder to check when finding it depends on memory. My starting point would be a small interview index. One row represents one conversation. The columns record the date, the speaker’s name, their role, the business, the main subjects and the location of the original notes. The index is a finding aid. It should point back to evidence rather than pretend to replace it. What belongs in the subject column? Plain words that I would actually search for: rent, delivery, training, winter trade, opening hours.

articles.body: Security testing is an essential part of software development. As applications become increasingly networked and deal with high volumes of sensitive information, finding security vulnerabilities early is important. Whatever software you're developing, whether it's a traditional web application, enterprise application or Web3 application, there are many risks relating to user information, financial transactions and downtime. The best way to approach this is to have security testing as a core part of your SDLC. This means that you can find and evaluate risks at each step of the development process. What Is Security Testing? Security testing is the process of identifying vulnerabilities, issues and misconfigurations that could be exploited within a software application.

articles.body: In 1964, Italian director Sergio Leone redefined the Western movie genre with A Fistful of Dollars . Eschewing the relatively simplistic morality tales of earlier films, Leone’s protagonist wasn’t a noble hero, but an opportunistic gunslinger who pits two rival Old West gangs against each other to score a big payday. Despite the moral complexity of it all — or, more likely, because of it — A Fistful of Dollars was an international success that proved three things: audiences were ready for a new kind of Western, America no longer had a monopoly on the genre, and Clint Eastwood was a bankable movie star.

articles.body: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California tonight (Nov. 11), the second such flight for the company in a six-day span. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:36 p.m. EST (8:36 p.m. local California time; 0136 GMT on Nov. 12), kicking off a mission called USSF-627. Vandenberg hosted a similar liftoff less than a week ago: On Nov. 6, a Falcon 9 sent the USSF-432 mission skyward from the site, which lies on California's gorgeous but often foggy central coast. A Falcon 9 first stage rests on a SpaceX drone ship shortly after launching the USSF-627 mission on Nov. 11, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) We don't know much about USSF-627 or USSF-432; both are classified.

articles.title: NASA kick-starts a fresh push to bring Mars samples home
articles.excerpt: NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for Mars Sample Return (MSR), called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture.
articles.body: A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet. NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth. The PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG).
articles.author: Leonard David

articles.title: We can't see Fast Radio Bursts but we can now hear them thanks to a Finnish Cathedral
articles.excerpt: Fast radio bursts are invisible, but a composer has turned thousands of them into sound at a Finnish cathedral, where a choir will sing along on Nov. 21.
articles.body: Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound. Fast radio bursts, or FRBs , are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star. Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space.
